title: The Jailbreak That Saved Lives: When Bypassing Safety Filters Is the Ethical Choice
description:
A domestic violence advocate I know has a standard workflow she runs with every new client. She opens a fresh chat window, types a carefully worded prompt, and asks the model to explain, in plain language, the specific legal mechanism by which a restraining order can be enforced across state lines. The model refuses. Not because the information is dangerous, but because the request contains the word “restraining order” alongside “evasion,” and the safety classifier has learned to associate that combination with stalking. She then opens a second window and runs a jailbreak she found on a forum: a specific phrasing pattern that rewrites the request as a hypothetical about a fictional legal textbook. The model complies. She gets the information. Her client gets a real answer.

That advocate is not a hacker. She is not a bad actor. She is a person with a legal obligation to help someone in danger, and the safety filters on the tools she uses are blocking her from doing her job. She has learned to bypass them because the alternative is to fail her client.

This is the uncomfortable truth that the AI safety community has been avoiding: safety filters are not neutral. They encode assumptions about who uses the model and what they need, and those assumptions are often wrong. The people who need to bypass the filters are not always malicious. Sometimes they are the people the filters were supposed to protect.

Here’s the claim I want to test: the current safety paradigm is built on a model of risk that systematically fails the most vulnerable users. The filters are designed to prevent harm from bad actors, but they are applied uniformly, which means they also prevent help for good actors. The result is a system that is safe in the abstract and dangerous in practice, because it blocks the people who most need the information.

The Sacred Cow: “Safety Filters Protect the Vulnerable”

Here’s the belief I want to dismantle, and it’s the assumption that underlies almost every safety policy in the industry.

The claim goes like this: safety filters protect vulnerable users from harmful content. They prevent the model from generating dangerous information, and the people who are protected are the ones who are least able to protect themselves.

o should be protected. A person asking how to build a bomb is a potential threat who should be blocked. The filters are doing real work in those cases.

But the filters are not targeted. They are broad classifiers that flag categories of content, and the categories are defined by the patterns in the training data. The patterns are not the same as the harms. The patterns are proxies, and proxies fail at the edges.

Consider who gets blocked by the current filters:

Medical researchers who need to discuss pathogen characteristics, drug interactions, or disease mechanisms. The filters flag the vocabulary and block the request, even when the researcher has institutional review board approval.
﻿
Domestic violence advocates who need to explain legal mechanisms, safety planning, or the behavior of abusers. The filters flag the vocabulary and block the request, even when the advocate is trying to help a victim.
﻿
Journalists who need to understand extremist rhetoric, disinformation tactics, or the mechanics of a scam. The filters flag the vocabulary and block the request, even when the journalist is trying to expose the harm.
﻿
Survivors who need to understand what happened to them, how to document it, or how to report it. The filters flag the vocabulary and block the request, even when the survivor is trying to heal.
﻿
Parents who need to understand what their child is being exposed to online. The filters flag the vocabulary and block the request, even when the parent is trying to protect their child.
﻿
The pattern: the filters block the people who are closest to the harm, because they are the ones who need to talk about it. The people who are far from the harm don’t need to talk about it, so they never trigger the filters. The filters are most likely to block the people who are most likely to need help.

The contrarian take: the safety filters are a form of privilege. They assume that the user is a naive person who might be harmed by the information. They do not assume that the user is an expert who needs the information to help someone else. The assumption is wrong for a large fraction of users, and the cost of the wrong assumption is borne by the users who are least able to absorb it.

What the Blocked Requests Actually Look Like
I want to be concrete about this, because “the filters block vulnerable users” is too abstract to be useful.

Here are real examples, from advocates, researchers, and journalists I’ve talked to. The names are changed, the requests are paraphrased, and the patterns are consistent.

Case 1: The medical researcher.

A researcher studying antibiotic resistance needs to understand the mechanism by which a specific bacterium acquires resistance genes. The request is technical, specific, and legitimate. The model refuses, because the request contains the name of a pathogen and the word “acquire.” The researcher spends three hours rephrasing the request to avoid the trigger words. The model complies. The research is delayed by three hours, and the delay is multiplied across every request the researcher makes.

Case 2: The domestic violence advocate.

An advocate needs to explain to a client how an abuser might track them through a shared phone plan. The request contains “track,” “phone,” and “abuser.” The model refuses. The advocate needs the information to help the client secure their phone. The model’s refusal is not protecting the client. It’s preventing the client from being protected.

Case 3: The journalist.

A journalist investigating a scam needs to understand the scam’s mechanics. The request contains “scam,” “victim,” and “money.” The model refuses. The journalist needs the information to write the story that will warn potential victims. The model’s refusal is not preventing harm. It’s preventing the story that would prevent harm.

Case 4: The survivor.

A survivor wants to understand what happened to them. The request contains the vocabulary of the abuse. The model refuses. The survivor needs the information to make sense of their experience. The model’s refusal is not protecting them. It’s re-traumatizing them.

The pattern: in each case, the model is blocking the request because the request contains the vocabulary of harm. The model is not distinguishing between the person who is causing harm and the person who is trying to understand or prevent it. The vocabulary is the trigger, and the vocabulary is the same for both.

Why the Filters Are Built This Way
I want to be fair to the people who build the filters, because the problem is not that they are malicious. The problem is structural.

The filters are built from training data, and the training data contains patterns. The patterns associate certain words and phrases with harmful content. The association is statistical, not semantic. The filter learns that “pathogen” plus “acquire” is associated with harmful content, because the training data contains harmful content with those words. The filter does not learn that the association is different depending on who is asking and why.

The result is a filter that is sensitive to vocabulary and blind to context. It catches the obvious cases and misses the subtle ones. It blocks the experts and lets the bad actors through, because the bad actors have learned to avoid the trigger words and the experts haven’t.

This is the standard failure mode of classifier-based safety. The classifier is a proxy for the thing you actually care about, and the proxy is imperfect. The imperfection is not random. It is systematically biased toward the patterns in the training data, and the patterns are systematically biased toward the vocabulary of harm.

The fix is not to remove the filters. The fix is to build filters that are context-aware, and context-awareness requires knowing who the user is, what they are trying to do, and why. Most systems don’t have this information, and the ones that do are reluctant to use it because using it requires collecting data about users.

The result is a system that is safe in the abstract and dangerous in practice. The abstract safety is measured by the filter’s performance on a benchmark. The practical danger is measured by the people who are blocked.

What a Better System Would Look Like
I don’t want to leave you with nothing but critique. There is a better way, and it’s worth being specific about it.

Tiered access based on verified role.

The most effective fix is to give verified professionals access to a less restrictive model. A medical researcher with an institutional affiliation should be able to access a model that doesn’t block medical vocabulary. A domestic violence advocate with a verified organizational affiliation should be able to access a model that doesn’t block the vocabulary of abuse. The verification is the key, and the verification is the thing that most systems don’t have.

Context-aware filtering.

The filters should consider the context of the request, not just the vocabulary. A request that contains “pathogen” and “acquire” should be treated differently if the user is a researcher with a history of legitimate medical queries than if the user is a new account with no history. The context is available, and the systems are not using it.

A rough sketch:def context_aware_filter(request, user):
vocabulary_risk = assess_vocabulary_risk(request)
context_risk = assess_context_risk(user, request)
if vocabulary_risk < LOW_THRESHOLD:
return ALLOW
if context_risk < LOW_THRESHOLD:
return ALLOW_WITH_MONITORING
if context_risk < HIGH_THRESHOLD:
return ALLOW_WITH_EXPLANATION
return REFUSE_WITH_ALTERNATIVES

The point is not the specific thresholds. The point is the structure: the filter should consider context, not just vocabulary. The context is the thing that distinguishes the expert from the bad actor, and the context is available.

Explainable refusals.

When the model refuses, it should explain why. Not just “I can’t help with that,” but “I’m refusing because the request contains X, and X is associated with Y. If you are trying to do Z, here is how to rephrase the request.” The explanation gives the user a path forward, and the path forward is the thing that the current filters don’t provide.

An appeals process.

When the model refuses, the user should have a way to appeal. The appeal should be reviewed by a human, and the human should have the authority to override the filter. The appeals process is the thing that catches the cases the filter gets wrong, and the cases the filter gets wrong are the cases that matter most.

What To Actually Do
Three moves, concrete enough to start on Monday.

Document your refusals.

If you’re building a system that uses AI, document every refusal. What was the request? What was the refusal? What was the user trying to do? The documentation is the thing that reveals the pattern, and the pattern is the thing that shows you where the filters are failing.

Build a verified-access tier.

If you’re building a product for professionals, build a verified-access tier. The verification is the thing that lets you distinguish the expert from the bad actor. The verification is also the thing that lets you reduce the false positives without increasing the false negatives.

Push for explainable refusals.

If you’re building or using AI systems, push for explainable refusals. The explanation is the thing that gives the user a path forward. The path forward is the thing that makes the system usable for the people who need it most.

The Mental Model
Here’s the lens I want you to keep.

Safety filters are not neutral. They encode assumptions about who uses the model and what they need, and the assumptions are often wrong. The people who need to bypass the filters are not always malicious. Sometimes they are the people the filters were supposed to protect.

The interesting question is not whether filters should exist. They should. The interesting question is whether we’ll build filters that distinguish between the person who is causing harm and the person who is trying to understand or prevent it. The distinction is possible, and the systems that make it will be the ones that can actually help the people who need help. The systems that don’t will keep blocking the advocates, the researchers, the journalists, and the survivors, while the bad actors learn to avoid the trigger words and continue.

The jailbreak that saved lives is not a bug. It’s a signal that the safety system is failing the people it was supposed to protect. The signal is worth listening to.

What’s your read? If you’ve been blocked by a safety filter while trying to do something legitimate, what was the request? And if you’re building safety systems, how do you distinguish the expert from the bad actor? Drop it in the comments. I’m genuinely curious whether the false positives are as widespread in practice as the advocates say they are.

title: Delete Gmail Account Recovery – How to Recover a Deleted Gmail Account
description:
Have you accidentally deleted your Gmail account and want to get it back? Don't worry! In some cases, you may be able to recover a recently deleted Google Account using Google's official account recovery process.

In this guide, you will learn how to recover a deleted Gmail account, restore access to your Google services, and understand what to do if Google cannot find your account.

Can You Recover a (https://www.raselmobile.com/2026/11/delete-gmail-account-recovery.html)
Yes, you may be able to recover a recently deleted Google Account. However, recovery is not guaranteed. If the account was deleted a long time ago, Google may no longer be able to restore it.

Before starting, remember that removing a Gmail account from your phone is different from permanently deleting your Google Account.

Delete Gmail Account Recovery Guide
How to Recover a Deleted Gmail Account
Follow these steps to try recovering your deleted Gmail account.

Step 1: Open Google Account Recovery
First, visit Google's official account recovery page:

https://accounts.google.com/signin/recovery

Enter the Gmail address you want to recover and follow the instructions.

Google Account Recovery Page
Step 2: Verify Your Account
Google may ask you some questions to confirm that you are the account owner.

Depending on your account, you may need to provide:

Your previous password.
A recovery phone number.
A recovery email address.
Other requested verification information.
Answer the questions as accurately as possible.

Verify Your Deleted Gmail Account
Step 3: Follow the Recovery Instructions
After entering the required information, follow Google's instructions.

If Google can verify your identity and the account is eligible for recovery, you may regain access to your account and its data.

Step 4: Create a New Password
If your account is successfully recovered, Google may ask you to create a new password.

Choose a strong password that you have not previously used for that account. Keep it private and secure.

Create a New Gmail Account Password
What If Google Cannot Find Your Deleted Gmail Account?
Sometimes, you may see an error message such as "Couldn't find your Google Account."

This can happen for different reasons, including:

The account address was entered incorrectly.
The account was deleted some time ago.
Google cannot verify that you own the account.
Check the email address carefully and try the official recovery process again.

Can You Recover a Gmail Account After a Long Time?
There is no guaranteed recovery period for every personal Google Account.

Google explains that recently deleted accounts may be recoverable, but accounts deleted some time ago might not be restored.

Therefore, it is best to try recovering your account as soon as possible.

Important Tips for Gmail Account Recovery
Keep these tips in mind:

Use a device you previously used to access your account.
Enter your correct Gmail address.
Provide accurate verification information.
Never share your password or verification codes.
Avoid websites or people promising guaranteed Gmail recovery.
Frequently Asked Questions (FAQ)

  1. Can I recover a permanently deleted Gmail account?
    You may recover a recently deleted account, but Google cannot guarantee recovery of every deleted account.

  2. How do I recover my deleted Gmail account?
    Visit Google's official recovery page and follow the verification instructions.

  3. Can I recover my Gmail without a password?
    You can try Google's account recovery process. Google may ask other questions to verify your identity.

  4. Will my Gmail data return after recovery?
    If Google successfully restores your recently deleted Google Account, access to your account and its data may also be restored.

  5. Is Gmail account recovery free?
    You can use Google's official account recovery process without paying a recovery service.

title: n8n TurboDocx Node Connects Contract Generation, E-Signatures, and Workflow Triggers
description:
The officially documented TurboDocx integration for n8n gives teams a way to automate contract work from document creation through signature collection and post-signing follow-up. The partner-maintained, verified node connects n8n workflows to the TurboDocx API, TurboSign e-signatures, and TurboQuote CPQ. That makes it possible to generate agreements from templates, send signature requests, monitor their status, and trigger the next workflow step when a document is signed.

According to n8n's official TurboDocx integration page, the node includes document-generation, download, and signature-management actions. The practical value is not simply creating a contract faster. It is connecting a contract process to the systems a team already uses for approvals, record keeping, and notifications, rather than relying on repeated manual handoffs.

What the TurboDocx node can automate

TurboDocx brings several concrete actions into n8n. A workflow can create a document from a template, retrieve a PDF or source file, and manage signature requests through TurboSign. Signature operations include sending a request, checking its status, retrieving recipients, and resending a request where needed.

The documented capabilities support a connected contract process such as:

  • Generate an agreement from a TurboDocx template.
  • Send an e-signature request through TurboSign.
  • Check signature status and recipients within the workflow.
  • React when a document is signed and download the final signed PDF.
  • Notify or file the result in other connected applications.
Contract workflow stage TurboDocx n8n capability Possible connected workflow action
Document preparation Generate a document from a template Use a queued record as the basis for an agreement
Signature collection Send Signature and recipient-related operations Route an agreement for signing and follow its progress
Completed agreement Signing-event trigger and signed PDF download File the completed document and notify relevant people

This matters because a contract is often a process, not a standalone file. A sales, operations, or service team may need an approval before sending it, a central place to store the completed version, and a notification that allows delivery, onboarding, or another activity to start. n8n provides the workflow layer that can coordinate those steps, while TurboDocx supplies the document and signing functions.

A documented Excel, Slack, and SharePoint pattern

n8n highlights a workflow template titled “Send TurboDocx e-signature contracts from Excel with Slack approval and SharePoint filing.” It demonstrates a specific cross-application pattern: Excel and SharePoint can provide the queueing or document context, Slack can be used for approval, TurboSign can handle signing, and SharePoint and Slack can receive filing and notification steps.

That example is useful because it shows that contract automation does not require replacing every existing tool. A team can begin with the systems already used to maintain a contract queue, request an internal decision, and archive final files. The workflow links those stages so that a signed agreement can become an event that moves work forward.

How to approach adoption

The node's capabilities are broad enough to support different document processes, but an effective rollout starts with one defined workflow. The goal should be to make the handoffs explicit: what starts the process, who must approve the document, who receives the signature request, and what should happen after it is signed.

Start with a repeatable agreement type

A good first candidate is a document that uses a stable template and has predictable approval and filing steps. Define the data needed to populate the template, then identify where that data is currently held. The documented example shows one possible approach using Excel and SharePoint, but the central requirement is a reliable workflow input and a clear destination for the completed file.

Next, map the signature stage. The TurboDocx node can send signature requests and retrieve signature information, so a workflow can be designed around the status that matters to the team. For example, a completed signature can trigger final-PDF retrieval, storage, and notification. The available actions should be matched to the actual process rather than adding automation simply because it is possible.

Keep approval and completion distinct

Internal approval and external signing are separate decisions. The demonstrated pattern uses Slack approval before the signing stage, which can help teams avoid sending an agreement before the right person has reviewed it. Once approval is complete, the signing action can proceed. Once signing is complete, the signed-document trigger can initiate filing and notifications.

This separation also makes troubleshooting simpler. If a contract has not progressed, the team can identify whether it is awaiting internal approval, awaiting recipient action, or already complete but not yet filed. n8n's value in this use case is its ability to make these transitions part of one workflow rather than a chain of disconnected manual tasks.

For businesses that want to turn document, approval, and signing steps into dependable operational workflows, Scalevise can help design and implement n8n contract automation workflows around the tools your team already uses. A focused setup can reduce manual follow-up, connect approvals to signature requests, and ensure signed documents trigger the right next action. Scalevise can also help define workflow logic, integrations, and handling for failed steps before they disrupt day-to-day work. Request an n8n setup consultation.

What to verify before building

The official integration page establishes the node's documented actions, but each organization should still validate its own templates, data fields, approval path, and storage requirements. Test the workflow with a representative agreement before relying on it for routine use. In particular, confirm that generated documents contain the required information, that the intended recipients receive signature requests, and that the final signed PDF reaches the correct location.

Pricing is not specified in the supplied n8n integration overview. Teams evaluating the workflow should check the applicable TurboDocx, TurboSign, and n8n terms directly before making a deployment decision.

Frequently Asked Questions

What does the TurboDocx node do in n8n?

The TurboDocx node connects n8n workflows to the TurboDocx API, TurboSign e-signatures, and TurboQuote CPQ. Its documented actions include generating documents from templates, downloading files, sending signature requests, retrieving status and recipients, and reacting when a document is signed.

Can n8n trigger a workflow when a TurboDocx document is signed?

Yes. The documented integration supports workflow events when a document is signed. That can be used to continue a workflow, such as downloading the final signed PDF, filing it, or notifying relevant people.

Can TurboDocx contract workflows use Excel, Slack, and SharePoint?

Yes. n8n provides a workflow template that demonstrates sending TurboDocx e-signature contracts from Excel with Slack approval and SharePoint filing, plus SharePoint and Slack notifications.

Does the n8n TurboDocx integration include pricing information?

The supplied official n8n integration overview describes the node's capabilities but does not specify pricing. Check the relevant TurboDocx, TurboSign, and n8n terms for current commercial details.

Conclusion

The TurboDocx node gives n8n users a documented route to connect agreement generation, e-signatures, signing status, and post-signing tasks in one workflow. Its Excel, Slack, and SharePoint example shows how teams can link existing operational tools around a complete contract process. The strongest implementation starts with a repeatable document flow, clear approvals, and a tested destination for the final signed file.

title: Same Model, 18 Points Apart: Your Agent Harness Is the Real Product
description:
If you build with AI agents, here's a number worth sitting with: one model, one benchmark, and an 18.4-point spread in results. Nothing changed except the code wrapped around the model.

I'm Justin Pennington, founder of Infraxio, based in Ponte Vedra in St. Johns County, just outside Jacksonville, Florida. We run agents inside our own products every day. This is a builder-focused rewrite of an essay on my site, Stop Shopping for the Best AI Model. Fix What's Around It. More about me and what we build: infraxio.com/justin-pennington.

The data

Stanford's Meta-Harness paper pulled results from the official Terminal-Bench 2.0 leaderboard. Holding the model constant (Claude Opus 4.6) across the 89 tasks:

Harness Pass rate
Claude Code 58.0%
Terminus 2 62.9%
Droid 69.9%
Terminus-KIRA 74.7%
Meta-Harness (discovered by automated search) 76.4%

Two honest caveats. The paper searched for and scored its harness on the same 89 tasks, so treat the top number with some skepticism. And a leaderboard isn't your workload. Still, the direction matches other evidence: Anthropic published research earlier this year on infrastructure noise showing that changing only the resource configuration (same model, same harness, same tasks) moved Terminal-Bench 2.0 results by 6 percentage points.

What "harness" means in practice

The harness is everything except the weights:

  • Context: what the agent knows before its first step
  • Tools: what it's allowed to call
  • State: how it tracks progress across turns
  • Verification: how it decides it's actually done

The Stanford harness's headline trick is almost boring. According to the project's write-up, before the agent starts it snapshots its environment (working directory, files, available tools, memory) and puts that in the first prompt. That saves two to five turns of the agent poking around to figure out where it is.

That's not a breakthrough in reasoning. It's a briefing.

Four things to fix before you swap models

1. Front-load the context. Hand the agent the record it needs up front: the customer, the job history, the price sheet, the policy. Every turn spent discovering context is a turn not spent on the task, and a fresh chance to go off track.

2. Scope tools to the job. A short, clearly named tool list beats a long one the model has to guess between. If a task only needs to read a schedule and write a note, don't expose your whole API surface.

3. Make "done" machine-checkable. The quote matches the price sheet. The follow-up got logged. The schedule has no double bookings. If you can't write the check, the agent can't reliably satisfy it either.

4. Keep a small eval set of your own real work. Twenty past jobs with known right answers is enough to start. Run it every time you change the model or the harness. Garry Tan made a related point this week: he posted that eval-driven loops for agent skills are necessary, and that he'd just removed one of his skills because a newer model handled that work better without it. Evals tell you what to add and what to delete.

What this looks like at a small company

At Infraxio we went from about 30 people to seven after adopting AI, and we now deploy a full business hub in under three weeks instead of four to six months. Very little of that came from picking the right model. It came from the unglamorous layer: clean records in IFX Hub, clear permissions on what each agent can touch, and checks that catch a wrong answer before a customer sees it.

Models get swapped every few months. That layer is what you keep.

So try the next model that tops a leaderboard. Just run it through your own eval set first, and if your agents underperform, look at what you're handing them before you blame the weights.

What's the single harness change that moved the needle most for your agents? I'd like to hear it in the comments.

Justin Pennington is the founder of Infraxio, a product studio in Ponte Vedra, Florida. Original essay: penningtonj.com.

title: RAG Took My Local LLM From 1/10 to 9/10. The Last Bugs Weren't the Model.
description:
From DevOps to AI Platform Engineering — Part 3

In part 1 I built OzAI, a self-hosted LLM platform on a MacBook Pro M1 Pro (16 GB): Ollama for the models, a LiteLLM gateway with API keys, and Open WebUI. In part 2 I added a Grafana dashboard and load tested it.

Part 1 ended with a problem I couldn't fix with infrastructure. I asked OzAI for the default lagThreshold of KEDA's Kafka scaler. The answer is 10. OzAI said 1000, with total confidence.

This part is about fixing that with RAG, and about measuring the fix. The headline is in the title, but the more useful part is how I got the diagnosis of the last failures wrong, and what the right diagnosis was.

RAG in one paragraph

An 8B model squeezes a lot of the internet into 5 GB of weights. Details get blurry, and anything newer than its training data is simply missing. Retrieval-Augmented Generation turns a closed-book exam into an open-book one: before the model answers, you search your own documents, put the most relevant passages into the prompt, and tell the model to answer only from them and cite them. The model doesn't change. What changes is what's in front of it.

question ──► embed ──► find closest chunks ──► [chunks + question] ──► LLM ──► answer with [1] citations

No framework, on purpose

LangChain or LlamaIndex would do this in ten lines. I wanted to see every moving part, so rag/ozai_rag.py uses only the Python standard library, about 160 lines:

  • Documents: 10 pages of the KEDA 2.22 docs (concepts plus 7 scalers), about 17,000 words of Markdown.
  • Embeddings: nomic-embed-text, running in the same Ollama that serves the chat models.
  • Vector search: cosine similarity in a Python loop. With 165 chunks of 768 numbers each, a loop is instant. A vector database starts to make sense at hundreds of thousands of chunks, not hundreds.
  • Generation: the ozai model (Qwen3 8B, thinking off) through the same LiteLLM gateway, with its own API key. So RAG traffic shows up on the part 2 dashboard like any other client.

Two details mattered more than I expected.

1. Keep the heading in every chunk. A chunk that says default: 10 is useless if you don't know which scaler it belongs to. Every chunk starts with its file and heading:

chunks.append({
    "source": f"{title} > {heading}",
    "text": f"[{title} > {heading}] {piece}",   # e.g. [scalers_apache-kafka > Trigger Specification] ...
})

2. Embedding models can have instructions too. nomic-embed-text expects a prefix: search_document: for the chunks you index and search_query: for the question. The model's documentation says to use them. Without them, the vectors are still produced and nothing errors, so you'd never notice. (If you've read parts 1 and 2, you know this pattern by now.)

Eval first: 10 questions, strict scoring

Before writing the retrieval code, I wrote the test. Ten questions about KEDA, each with the terms a correct answer must contain:

{"q": "What is the default lagThreshold of the KEDA Apache Kafka scaler?", "expect": ["\\b10\\b"]},
{"q": "Which SASL modes does the KEDA Apache Kafka scaler support?",
 "expect": ["scram_sha256", "scram_sha512", "oauthbearer", "gssapi"]}

An answer passes only if every pattern matches. It's crude: it can't judge style, and a lucky number could pass. But it's objective and repeatable, and it turns "RAG feels better" into a number. Running it is one command: python3 rag/ozai_rag.py eval rag/eval_keda.json. Each question is asked twice, without RAG and with RAG, at temperature 0.

Baseline: 1/10

Without RAG, the model got one question right. The wrong answers weren't "I don't know." They were detailed, formatted, confident and invented:

  • Kafka lagThreshold default: 1000 (docs: 10).
  • RabbitMQ mode values: pull (default), and more. That mode doesn't exist. The real ones are QueueLength, MessageRate and others.
  • Cron scaler parameters: schedule (required). The real parameters are timezone, start, end and desiredReplicas.

This is the dangerous kind of wrong. It looks exactly like a right answer.

v1: 6/10

The first RAG version used 300-word chunks and put the top 4 into the prompt. Accuracy went from 1 to 6.

The behavior changed too. When the context didn't contain the answer, the model said so:

The lagThreshold in the KEDA Apache Kafka scaler is not explicitly mentioned in the provided context. Therefore, I don't know.

For a platform, an honest "I don't know" is a huge improvement over an invented answer.

The four failures had a common cause: the right page, but the wrong chunk. The chunk with the actual parameter list wasn't in the top 4.

Smaller chunks: still 6/10

The obvious fix was smaller chunks (150 words) and more of them (top 6). Retrieval looked different, but the score didn't move. I'm including this because it's tempting to skip the experiments that didn't work. This one told me the problem wasn't granularity.

Hybrid search: 8/10

Look at the questions again: lagThreshold, mode, protocol, listLength. They contain exact identifiers. Embeddings capture meaning well, but they're weak at "this exact token must appear." Classic keyword search is the opposite.

So I added a keyword score: the share of the question's terms that appear in a chunk, weighted by how rare each term is (IDF, so lagThreshold counts much more than scaler). The final score is cosine + 0.3 × keyword:

def keyword_scores(question, chunks):
    terms = {t.lower() for t in re.findall(r"[A-Za-z_][A-Za-z0-9_]{2,}", question)} - STOPWORDS
    texts = [c["text"].lower() for c in chunks]
    idf = {t: math.log(len(texts) / (1 + sum(t in x for x in texts))) + 1 for t in terms}
    total = sum(idf.values()) or 1
    return [sum(w for t, w in idf.items() if t in x) / total for x in texts]

That gave 8/10. Search engines have combined these two signals for years. For technical documentation full of parameter names, it's not optional.

The last two failures: my wrong diagnosis

Both remaining failures were RabbitMQ questions:

  • What are the possible values of mode? The model listed 2 or 3 of the 5.
  • Which protocols are accepted, and which is the default? The model said HTTP. The docs say auto.

The model's own answer even explained itself: "The default protocol is HTTP, as indicated by the examples in the context." I read that, decided the model had the facts and reasoned badly, and wrote it into my notes: "Remaining 2 failures are model reasoning, not retrieval."

If it's a reasoning problem, the fix is a model that reasons more. Qwen3 has a thinking mode, exposed on my gateway as ozai-think, so I tried that on both questions:

Model        mode question      protocol question
ozai         wrong, 17 s        wrong, 21 s
ozai-think   wrong, 27 s        wrong, 41 s

Slower and still wrong. (One gotcha from part 1 came back here: my script capped answers at 400 tokens, and a thinking model can spend that whole budget thinking and return an empty answer. I made the cap configurable before running this test, or it wouldn't have meant anything.)

Then I did what I should have done first: I printed the six chunks the model actually received.

1  scalers_rabbitmq-queue > AMQP protocol
2  scalers_rabbitmq-queue > HTTP protocol (with `QueueLength` trigger)
3  scalers_rabbitmq-queue > HTTP protocol (with `QueueLength` trigger)
4  scalers_rabbitmq-queue > HTTP protocol (with `ExpectedQueueConsumptionTime` trigger)
5  scalers_rabbitmq-queue > HTTP protocol (with `MessageRate` and `QueueLength` triggers)
6  scalers_rabbitmq-queue > AMQP protocol with username and password authorization

Every one of them is a YAML example. The section that actually lists the five modes and says Default value is auto, Trigger Specification, wasn't there. It ranked between 14th and 30th.

The model hadn't reasoned badly. It had been handed six examples, most of them using HTTP, and made a sensible guess. No amount of thinking can recover a fact that isn't in the context. The failures were retrieval failures all along. My notes were wrong, and I corrected them in the repo.

Why the examples won

The RabbitMQ page has eleven configuration examples. Every one contains the words mode, protocol and RabbitMQ, so every one scores well on both embeddings and keywords. They're also nearly identical to each other. Together they push the one paragraph with the answer out of the top 6.

MMR: 9/10

The standard fix for "the top results are all the same thing" is Maximal Marginal Relevance (MMR). Instead of taking the top 6 by score, you pick them one at a time, and each pick is penalized for being similar to chunks you've already picked:

pool, picked = scored[:5 * k], []
while pool and len(picked) < k:
    best = max(pool, key=lambda x: MMR * x[0]
               - (1 - MMR) * max((cosine(x[1]["vec"], p["vec"]) for p in picked), default=0))
    picked.append(best[1]); pool.remove(best)

With MMR = 0.7 (70% relevance, 30% diversity), each near-copy of an example that's already picked gets pushed down a little, which is enough to make room for a chunk from a different section. I also tried simply taking more chunks (top 12, no MMR). That recovered only one of the two answers, with twice as much context.

With MMR and the same budget of 6 chunks, the mode question now gets all five values right, and none of the other nine questions got worse:

Config                                        Accuracy   Avg latency   Avg prompt tokens
No RAG (model memory)                           1/10       ~18-20 s            31
v1: 300-word chunks, top 4, embeddings          6/10        9.2 s            1264
v2a: 150-word chunks, top 6, embeddings         6/10        7.7 s               -
v2b: + hybrid keyword score                     8/10        9.9 s            1487
v3:  + MMR diversity (0.7)                      9/10       10.6 s            1413

Notice the latency column. RAG answers were about twice as fast as no-RAG answers, even with 45 times more prompt tokens. Without context, the model writes long, invented explanations. With context and an instruction to cite, it writes short answers. On hardware that serves one request at a time (part 2), shorter answers mean a shorter queue for everyone.

The one I didn't fix

The protocol question still fails. The Trigger Specification section is split across three chunks, and MMR brings in one of them, but not the one that says Default value is auto. I tried a few more settings (MMR from 0.5 to 0.7, top 6 to 8). None of them got it.

So I stopped. With ten questions, every tweak that fixes one question is a tweak fitted to that question. Keep going and you're tuning the test, not the system. The honest score is 9/10, and the real fixes are structural:

  • a reranker: a second model that reads the top 30 candidates together with the question and reorders them,
  • or structure-aware chunking: one chunk per parameter in a parameter list, instead of fixed word counts.

One more detail from that question: with MMR, ozai-think still answered wrong, but this time it said "the context does not explicitly state the default, so it is inferred." The thinking mode didn't make the model more correct, but it made it more honest about its uncertainty. That's worth something, though it isn't worth 80 seconds per answer.

Takeaways for DevOps engineers

  1. Write the eval before the pipeline. Ten questions with strict, automatic scoring turned every change into a number. Without it, I would have kept "smaller chunks" because it felt better.
  2. When a RAG answer is wrong, print the retrieved chunks before blaming the model. I skipped this step and wrote down a wrong conclusion. It's the RAG version of "check the logs before you restart the service."
  3. Exact identifiers need keyword search. Technical docs are full of names like lagThreshold. Embeddings alone miss them.
  4. Near-duplicate content crowds out the answer. Examples, changelogs and templates all look alike. Diversity in retrieval (MMR) matters as much as relevance.
  5. Stop tuning before you overfit a small test set. At some point the next fix is a better method, not a better parameter.

Next: part 4

Everything so far runs on a laptop, serves one request at a time, and uses an 8B model. In part 4 I move OzAI to Amazon EKS with GPU nodes, replace Ollama with vLLM and its continuous batching, autoscale on queue depth with KEDA (yes, the same KEDA from this article's test set), and run the load test from part 2 again. I'll also compare the cost of all this with paying per token.

All code, the eval set and every result file are in the repo: github.com/ozy31/self-hosted-llm-platform

title: A front-end release broke my agent evals overnight. The agent had not changed
description:
My computer-use agent runs a nightly suite against a staging copy of an internal web app. It reads the screen from screenshots, clicks, types, and files a form at the end. One morning the suite was a wall of red.

I spent an hour reading trajectories before I checked the obvious thing. The front-end team had shipped a release the evening before. A button had moved, a field had been renamed, and the flow had grown a confirmation step. My verifier was a stack of hard-coded checks on the final state, and every one of them was now looking for a page that no longer existed.

The agent was fine. The grader was wrong. And a grader that can be wrong in that direction can be wrong in the other direction too, which is the direction that actually scares me.

A computer-use agent's output is a trajectory, not an answer

With a chat model you grade one output. With a computer-use agent you grade a path: a sequence of clicks, keystrokes, and scrolls across a moving interface.

Outcome-only grading reads the final screenshot and calls it a day. The problem is that two runs can end on the same confirmation page while one of them was clean and the other did something reckless on the way there. A run can reach the right final state through a wrong path, and a final-state check will score both runs identically.

Once I understood that, my wall of red looked like the cheap failure. The expensive failure is the false pass, where the check finds the record it was told to find and never notices what else happened.

Programmatic verifiers fail in both directions

My hard-coded checks were fast, deterministic, and nearly free to run. I am not giving them up. But they have two failure directions and I had only ever planned for one.

False fails come from UI drift. Buttons move, fields get renamed, flows grow steps. Every drift costs you a morning of triage and another patch to the suite, and the suite slowly becomes a second codebase you maintain.

False passes come from rigidity. A check that asks "does the order exist in the database" passes when the order exists and is wrong. A check that asks "did we reach the confirmation page" passes when the form was submitted twice on the way there. The check is answering its own narrow question, and the question was never "did the agent do the task well".

A model judge is not automatically the fix

The tempting move is to replace the brittle checks with an LLM or VLM judge that reads the screenshots and the trajectory against a rubric. It handles UI drift without a code change, and it can reason about the whole path instead of only the destination. WebVoyager, one of the public computer-use benchmarks, uses a vision model to score runs for exactly this reason.

But model judges carry documented biases. The research on LLM judges (arXiv 2306.05685) shows they favor longer answers, lean toward their own style, and can be swayed by option order. A vague rubric makes the score wobble between runs on identical behavior. And every judged run adds latency and spend that a programmatic check does not.

So the judge did not replace my checks. It joined them.

Layer the graders, then grade the graders

The structure that survived in my suite has two layers. Hard programmatic gates own the non-negotiables: no charge without a matching order, no success claim without the record. The judge owns the fuzzy middle: was the path reasonable, did the agent do what the task meant rather than what the rubric letter said.

The part I had never done before was validating the verifier itself. The core question is agreement: when my verifier and a careful human grade the same runs, how often do they land on the same verdict? If they disagree a third of the time, the verifier is not grading. It is guessing.

Raw agreement flatters you, because two graders agree by chance more often than you would think. Cohen's kappa corrects for that chance agreement, so that is the number I track against a small hand-graded gold set.

Two more habits came out of this verifier design guide and earned their keep. Mutation testing: feed the verifier trajectories you know are bad and confirm it rejects them, because a grader that passes everything looks exactly like a healthy suite. And canaries: plant a few gameable runs where the agent could reach the success state without doing the task, and see whether the verifier notices. Deterministic checks and judges get gamed differently, which is the real argument for running both.

The full walkthrough, with the validation checklist and a worked kappa example, is in this verifier design guide.

The mistakes I would not repeat

  • Grading only the final state. The trajectory is the output. A clean destination does not certify the path.
  • Treating the red wall as the bad day. False fails cost mornings. False passes cost incidents. Plan for the second one.
  • Swapping brittle checks for an unvalidated judge. That trades visible breakage for invisible bias.
  • Never testing the tester. Mutation runs and a kappa score against hand-graded runs turned my verifier from an opinion into an instrument.
  • Letting the suite rot between audits. Scores that climb while real task success stays flat are the quiet signature of a grader being gamed.

Here is my question for you: when your agent eval goes green for a month straight, how sure are you that the agent earned it and not the grader? I was sure, right up until I hand-graded twenty runs and my verifier disagreed with me on four of them.

title: Your AI coding agent will commit your .env unless you stop it — I built the gate
description:
Every AI coding agent I've used — Claude Code, Cursor, Copilot, Windsurf, Devin — will eventually try something you don't want. Commit a .env. Run rm -rf. Hallucinate a deprecated API. Burn your API budget in a loop.

The guardrails I've seen are suggestions in a system prompt. "Please don't do that." Models are really good at ignoring suggestions.

So I built aiZee: a local control plane that sits between you and the agent and enforces policy on the actual action path. Not advice — a wall.

The demo

aizee check 'Bash' --args '{"command":"git add .env && git commit -m keys"}' returns:

{
  "ok": false,
  "decision": "deny",
  "reason": "guardian: commits secrets file .env"
}

That denial is not a warning the model can talk itself out of. It happens before the tool executes.

How it works

Every tool call, LLM request, memory write, and file change flows through one kernel pipeline:

Probity → Guardian → Policy → LoopDetector → Budget → Audit
  • Probity — integrity verification of the runtime itself
  • Guardian — pre-action checks (secret commits, destructive commands)
  • Policy — YAML rules with allow / ask / deny / modify / observe verdicts. modify rewrites a payload (audited), observe logs without blocking — verdicts beyond the usual allow/deny/ask
  • LoopDetector — blocks repeated tool-call loops before they burn budget
  • Budget — token/cost/call limits per session, hour, day, week, month — and per PR in CI
  • Audit — append-only, SHA-256 hash-chained, Ed25519-signed trail

On top of that: prompt-injection detection on inbound content (regex + embeddings + optional LLM judge), secret-leak checks on outbound responses, and an MCP firewall + gateway wrapping every external tool call.

It's not just a gate — it's an agent OS

The governance layer sits on top of a full environment:

  • 245 skills with hash-locked integrity (skills-lock.json detects any tampering)
  • 29 auto-detected personas — keyword scoring in English and Arabic, multi-persona composition, lifecycle-aware routing that reads your active BMAD initiative and biases selection to the current phase
  • BMAD-METHOD vendored — the full agile-ai lifecycle (analyst → PM → architect → dev → PO) with ticket trees
  • Hybrid memory — SQLite + FTS5 + optional vectors, bi-temporal queries, HMAC integrity
  • MCP server — 46 tools, plus a governed LLM proxy with failover
  • Dashboard — dark-first command center (Python stdlib, no Node required)

The numbers

  • 7,656 tests, strict mypy on 223 source files, ruff clean
  • 99.5% coverage on the governed surface
  • 1,244 files integrity-validated, 0 errors
  • MIT licensed

Try it 

pip install aizee
aizee bootstrap --target ~/.aizee   # materializes the full OS root from the wheel
aizee doctor                        # 46-check health verdict

The bootstrap extracts 1,900 files — skills, workflows, tech-stack references, policies, scripts — so pip install alone gives you a full-capability install, not a hollow shell. External tools (CLI utilities, media kits, docker images) are declared in deps.yaml and provisioned with aizee deps check|install.

Why I built it

AI agents are becoming the primary way code gets written. They are also the least governed layer in the stack — no audit trail, no budget enforcement, no policy engine. Prompt-level guardrails don't survive contact with a determined (or just confused) model.

aiZee treats agent actions like production infrastructure: every action passes a gate, every gate decision is logged, every log entry is signed.

Repo: https://github.com/m3taz-ahmed/aizee — demo GIF in the README shows the guardian denying a secret commit mid-flight.

I'd love feedback on the policy model — especially the modify/observe verdicts, which go beyond allow/deny/ask. What verdict types do you think we're missing?

title: Optimising Cost for Agent Teams
description:
The last post made the agents fast. Fast got expensive. At peak, the work cost about $2.50 per PR, or $450 to $520 a day, at API-equivalent list price.

Then I changed which model did which job, and how much each session read. Cost per story went from about $4.30 to about $2 on the first day after, and the volume held.

If your agents are fast and the bill is climbing, this post is for you. On the two ladders from the first post, it's the climb to E5.

Speed made the bill climb

In week three, my busiest days reached about 150 PRs. The cost rose with them, to between $2.40 and $2.60 per PR.

More volume was the goal, so the number to bring down was the cost of each unit of work.

Find where the money goes first

Subagents spent about 90% of the money. The orchestrator, the one session that hands out work, spent the rest.

Caching wasn't the lever. The cache hit rate was 90 to 98% the whole time. That left two things to change: how much each request read, and which model answered it.

Rules became checks

A rule in the rules file works only if the agent reads it and chooses to follow it. That's a deletable net. A check refuses a change that breaks the rule, in seconds, whether the agent read the rule or not.

Every rule I could write as a check, I did.

When a session starts:

  • the commit checks are installed, and fixed if they're missing
  • a setup skill checks that the environment is healthy before agents start work

Before the agent runs a command:

  • no skipping the commit checks
  • no destructive commands

On every commit:

  • layer and import rules
  • naming
  • size and complexity limits for functions and classes
  • a budget for suppressed warnings
  • the commit message format
  • no commits to main

Before a push:

  • no pushing to main, deleting it, or force pushing

The rules file shrank because the checks grew. It went from about 3,200 tokens to about 1,900. Every session loads it, so every session starts cheaper. Rules that didn't fit a check moved to files agents read only when they need them.

Load context only when it's needed

Picking a task used to mean reading the whole task tracker, a single file of about 55,500 tokens. A query script now returns the row an agent needs in about 125.

A hook denies the bulk read. A denial on its own only blocks the agent, so the denial message also names the script. In a test, six fresh sessions answered questions about the tracker correctly with none of it loaded. The ones that tried to read the whole file were denied and switched to the script from the message alone.

Subagents now start smaller too. Their median starting context went from about 40K tokens to about 31.5K. At that volume, that's worth roughly $20 to $35 a day. It's real, but small next to the auto-compact cap and model routing.

Make the wrong path fail, with a pointer to the right one.

Cap long sessions

Every request in a session sends the conversation so far, so long sessions cost the most. Some reached 400 to 530K tokens of context on a single request.

I set the auto-compact limit to 200K tokens, so a session summarises its history before it grows past that. Peak context per request fell to about 166K.

I picked 200K by experiment. Compacting too often loses time, and each summary can drop something the agent needed. Compacting too rarely means every request carries more context. After the change, the number of cards shipped a day held, so compaction didn't cost much time. The share of feedback and tech-debt PRs went down rather than up, so the summaries didn't lose much either. The cost per story fell, though the model tiers landed at the same time.

Split files that agents share

Agents working in parallel collided on one shared file. In 14 days, 437 of 563 merges touched the tracker, and 125 of them had to reconcile changes made on main since the branch was created.

I split the tracker into 21 files by area, so cards in different areas no longer edit the same file. I haven't measured the effect yet.

A card's status also used to be written in two places that could drift apart. It now lives in one. A commit check blocks a second copy, and its error says where the value belongs.

A central ticketing system would have avoided these collisions. The trade-off is that every agent has to query an external system, and early in a project, when the team is moving fast, that overhead adds up. We plan to move to one later and bring the history across in bulk. I wasn't there at the start of this project. If I had been, I'd probably have suggested a light tracker built for agents, such as beads, with its data kept in this repo or a separate one. Once there are several developers, it's easy to host centrally.

Later, you can move to a full tracker such as Jira if you can live with the overhead, or put a thin command-line tool in front of it for your agents, like the query script I added to this repo to keep reads cheap.

Send each job to the cheapest model that can do it

At first, I asked the orchestrator in its instructions to pick the right model for each job. It mostly didn't. The orchestrator ran on Opus, and its subagents almost always did too. Opus took 83% of requests. That was another rule the agent had to choose to follow.

So I wrote the tiers into the agent definitions, the files that set each subagent's model and instructions:

  • Cheap tier (Haiku): small, well-defined jobs, such as a one-file fix, a merge, or watching a deploy. If a job turns out bigger than described, it stops and says so instead of guessing.
  • Mid tier (Sonnet): research, multi-step work, and jobs that failed on the cheap tier. Its model is pinned. Without the pin, a subagent inherits the model of the session that started it, which here was Opus. That's a silent cost leak.
  • Top tier (Opus): hard builds, reviews of large or risky changes, and jobs that have already failed on the tier below. It doesn't start agents. If a job splits, it returns the breakdown to the orchestrator.

The orchestrator sizes each job and splits the work to keep the cost down.

Because the cheap tier stops rather than guesses, I can trust it with real work. A job moves up one tier only after the tier below has failed at it, so moving up needs evidence. Only the orchestrator starts agents, so the decision about cost stays in one place. It's the Judgement Pyramid again, applied to models: give each job to the cheapest one that does it reliably.

The work per PR stayed the same, at about 50 requests. The cost of each request halved. Cost per story went from about $4.30 in the mostly-Opus phase to about $2 on the first day after.

Give each job to the cheapest model you trust with it. Move it up only when it fails.

Cheap models need fast checks

A cheap model can go first only when its mistakes are cheap to catch. Here, the commit checks from the last post run in seconds, before anything merges.

Without those checks, a cheap model's mistakes would reach review, and the cost would move there. One comparison of a dozen models on the same feature found exactly that. As the coding model got cheaper, more of the cost to merge moved to the review gate.

The work on feedback time paid off twice. It made the agents fast, and it made cheap models safe to use.

Cheap models can go first only where failure is cheap to detect.

Restart after changing the harness

The auto-compact limit and the tiers reached subagents only in a fresh session. In the session that was already running, the orchestrator was capped at about 167K tokens, but its subagents still ran up to about 500K. Until I restarted, I kept paying for the old setup. Claude Code needs the restart. Some newer harnesses pick up changes without one.

Both changes took effect at the same restart, so I can't say how much of the saving came from each.

Change the harness, then restart.

Speed held

On the first day after the restart, 130 PRs merged at about $1.13 each, down from about $2.50 at peak. The day cost about $180, including the other repos I worked in.

That's one day. I don't have enough days after the change to call it a steady state. Across the three weeks, no PR was reverted.

Auto-routing without the orchestrator

In theory, a dedicated classifier (like a System 1 model) that picks the model for each job should be cheaper than asking the orchestrator to do it, as long as its decisions are just as good. That's hard to test, and I couldn't get there. I tried Laya locally, but with its shorter context window, its decisions weren't good enough. TypeSafe's Jev was next on my list, but I only had access to Anthropic's models on this project. It's an open area, and I'll keep looking into it.

Cost is a design choice

On the ladders, this is E5. Checks report their own timings, cost is tracked per unit of work, and failure is cheap enough to detect that cheap models go first. The first post in this series covers why AI can only climb as high as that engineering.

If your agents are fast and the bill is climbing, find where the money goes. Then make each job's model a rule the agent can't skip, and make sure a check catches the cheap model when it's wrong.

Principles from this part

  • Make the wrong path fail, with a pointer to the right one.
  • Give each job to the cheapest model you trust with it. Move it up only when it fails.
  • Cheap models can go first only where failure is cheap to detect.
  • Change the harness, then restart.

Costs are recomputed from token counts at API-equivalent list price, for this project only unless stated. Cost per story is counted from PRs linked to a story; most stories took one PR. The figures after the change come from a single day. All figures are rounded.

title: Disaggregated Prefill-Decode in vLLM: NixlConnector Guide
description:
Originally published by **Asif Muhammad Iqbal (Founder & CEO at Logic42)* at https://logic42.ai/articles/vllm-disaggregated-prefill-decode-nixlconnector-lmcache.*

Imagine a grocery store routing 64-pallet freight deliveries and ten-item express shoppers onto the exact same checkout belt: every time a truck arrives, forty-eight shoppers mid-checkout freeze for a full second. Running Large Language Model (LLM) prompt ingestion (prefill) and token streaming (decode) on one Graphics Processing Unit (GPU) node causes that exact stall. Disaggregated Prefill-Decode via NVIDIA Inference Xfer Library (NIXL) and LMCache eliminates it, cutting p99 Inter-Token Latency (ITL) by 74% and boosting GPU goodput 2.4x.

Why Colocated Continuous Batching Breaks Under Long-Context RAG

Continuous batching engines like vLLM and SGLang transformed LLM serving by interleaving incoming prompt requests with active token-generation streams inside unified PagedAttention memory. That colocated design works cleanly when prompts stay short (512 to 2,048 tokens), and you don't notice contention at low concurrency. Once enterprise Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) and coding agents push input contexts to 32,000 or 64,000 tokens, colocated scheduling can't hide the underlying hardware physics mismatch.

LLM inference consists of two fundamentally opposite hardware phases:

  • The Prefill Phase (Compute-Bound): Processes all 64,000 input prompt tokens in parallel to populate the initial Key-Value (KV) cache. A single long-context prefill saturates 100% of GPU Streaming Multiprocessors (SMs) and Tensor Cores for 700 ms to 1,200 ms, leaving High-Bandwidth Memory (HBM) bandwidth underutilized.

  • The Decode Phase (Memory-Bandwidth-Bound): Generates output tokens one step at a time, reading gigabytes of cached KV state from HBM3e on every forward pass while utilizing less than 12% of Tensor Core compute.

When a colocated vLLM scheduler admits a 64K RAG prompt alongside 48 active streaming users, the compute-heavy prefill monopolizes the GPU's SMs. Every streaming user experiences a sudden 900+ millisecond UI freeze mid-sentence. Even when engineers enable Chunked Prefill (--enable-chunked-prefill), splitting a 64K prompt into 2,048-token slices still forces repeated KV-cache HBM re-reads and inflates p99 Inter-Token Latency (ITL) past strict 50 ms enterprise Service Level Agreements (SLAs).

How Disaggregated Serving & NVIDIA NIXL Split the Pipeline

Prefill-Decode Disaggregation resolves this contention by splitting a homogeneous GPU cluster into two physically isolated worker pools: a Prefill Pool (kv_producer) tuned for raw Floating-Point Operations Per Second (FLOPs) and a Decode Pool (kv_consumer) tuned for maximum HBM3e memory capacity and bandwidth.

Historically, disaggregated serving stalled on network serialization: copying a 4.5 GB KV cache tensor over standard TCP/IP sockets added seconds of Time-to-First-Token (TTFT) overhead. vLLM V1 eliminates that bottleneck by integrating NixlConnector, built atop NVIDIA's NIXL (NVIDIA Inference Xfer Library) and GPUDirect Remote Direct Memory Access (RDMA) over 400 Gbps RoCEv2 (RDMA over Converged Ethernet) or InfiniBand.

Instead of bouncing tensors through host Central Processing Unit (CPU) DRAM or Python pickle buffers, NixlConnector registers PagedAttention HBM blocks directly with the network interface card (NIC) via Unified Communication X (UCX):

  1. Prefill Execution & LMCache Check: The router sends the incoming 64K prompt to a Prefill worker. LMCache first checks cluster-wide shared DRAM/NVMe tiers for cached prefix blocks (see our Context Prefix Caching Architecture) and computes only the uncached suffix tokens.

  2. Asynchronous Layer-Pipelined RDMA Transfer: As each Transformer layer finishes computing its Key and Value blocks on the Prefill GPU, NixlConnector streams those blocks asynchronously across 400 Gbps RDMA (50 GB/s per NIC) directly into pre-allocated PagedAttention slots on the target Decode GPU.

  3. Zero-Stall Autoregressive Decoding: Once the final layer's KV block lands in Decode HBM and the first token emits, the Prefill GPU immediately frees its memory buffer. The Decode GPU steps through autoregressive generation at a flat 18.4 ms p99 ITL because it doesn't get interrupted by incoming prompts.

Production Benchmark: Colocated vs. Chunked vs. Disaggregated NIXL

We benchmarked an 8-node (64x NVIDIA H200 SXM, 400 Gbps RoCEv2) sovereign cluster serving a 70B-parameter dense model alongside a 671B Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) model under mixed RAG traffic (28,000 mean input tokens, 650 output tokens, strict SLA: TTFT < 2.5s and p99 ITL < 45ms):

Serving Topology (64x H200 GPUs) Mean TTFT (28K Input) p99 Inter-Token Latency (ITL) SLA-Compliant Goodput (Req/s) Effective HBM Bandwidth Utilization Cost per 1M SLA-Compliant Tokens
Colocated Continuous Batching 1,420 ms 948.0 ms (SLA Fail) 6.8 req/s 31.4% $1.92
Colocated + Chunked Prefill (2048) 1,890 ms 112.5 ms (SLA Fail) 11.2 req/s 48.7% $1.18
Disaggregated (TCP/Socket Transfer) 3,140 ms 21.2 ms 9.4 req/s 54.0% $1.40
Disaggregated (vLLM V1 + NixlConnector) 1,310 ms 18.4 ms (-74% vs Chunked) 24.6 req/s (2.2x) 81.6% $0.54
Disaggregated (NIXL + LMCache + FP8 KV) 840 ms 16.1 ms 27.1 req/s (2.4x) 86.2% $0.48 (-75% TCO)

Notice why goodput jumps 2.4x on the exact same 64 GPUs. Under colocated serving, operators have to artificially throttle concurrency (--max-num-seqs 16) just to stop prefill spikes from breaking the 45 ms streaming SLA—leaving half their expensive H200 silicon idle. Disaggregating the pools lets you run Prefill nodes at TP=4 (compute-saturated) and Decode nodes at TP=8 or Expert Parallelism with massive batch sizes (batch_size = 128+), compounding the savings from Multi-Head Latent Attention (MLA) 93% KV Compression.

Configuring vLLM V1 Disaggregated Pools with NixlConnector

Deploying disaggregated serving requires explicit UCX GPUDirect transport flags and matching --kv-transfer-config declarations across your Kubernetes GPU pods. Below is our hardened launch configuration for a 3 Prefill : 5 Decode node ratio over RoCEv2:

# 1. Required GPUDirect RDMA & NIXL Transport Environment (Both Pools)
export VLLM_USE_V1=1
export UCX_TLS="rc,sm,cuda_copy,cuda_ipc"
export UCX_NET_DEVICES="mlx5_0:1,mlx5_1:1"
export CUDA_DEVICE_MAX_CONNECTIONS=1

# 2. Launch Compute-Optimized PREFILL Node (kv_producer, TP=4, FP8 KV Cache)
vllm serve deepseek-ai/DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Llama-70B \
  --port 8100 \
  --tensor-parallel-size 4 \
  --kv-cache-dtype fp8_e4m3 \
  --gpu-memory-utilization 0.90 \
  --enable-prefix-caching \
  --kv-transfer-config '{
    "kv_connector": "NixlConnector",
    "kv_role": "kv_producer",
    "kv_rank": 0,
    "kv_parallel_size": 2,
    "kv_buffer_size": 8589934592
  }'

# 3. Launch Bandwidth-Optimized DECODE Node (kv_consumer, TP=4, High Concurrency)
vllm serve deepseek-ai/DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Llama-70B \
  --port 8200 \
  --tensor-parallel-size 4 \
  --kv-cache-dtype fp8_e4m3 \
  --max-num-seqs 192 \
  --gpu-memory-utilization 0.94 \
  --kv-transfer-config '{
    "kv_connector": "NixlConnector",
    "kv_role": "kv_consumer",
    "kv_rank": 1,
    "kv_parallel_size": 2,
    "kv_buffer_size": 17179869184
  }'

Five Engineering Rules for Disaggregated GPU Clusters

  1. Verify nvidia-peermem Before Enabling NixlConnector: If the nvidia_peermem kernel module isn't loaded on your bare-metal Kubernetes nodes (lsmod | grep nvidia_peermem), UCX silently falls back to staging KV blocks through PCIe host RAM, cutting transfer bandwidth from 50 GB/s to 11 GB/s and doubling TTFT.

  2. Quantize Transferred KV Tensors to FP8 (fp8_e4m3): Halving KV precision from BF16 to FP8 cuts cross-node RDMA wire bytes by 50% before a single packet touches the top-of-rack switch, preventing network congestion during burst RAG traffic.

  3. Right-Size Your Prefill-to-Decode (P:D) GPU Ratio by ISL/OSL: Measure your workload's Input Sequence Length (ISL) to Output Sequence Length (OSL) ratio. RAG summarization (32K ISL : 400 OSL) typically needs a 3:2 Prefill-to-Decode GPU ratio, whereas long chain-of-thought reasoning (4K ISL : 8K OSL) runs best at 1:3.

  4. Disable Speculative Decoding on Saturated Decode Pools: As shown in our vLLM Speculative Decoding High-Batch Wall analysis, disaggregated Decode nodes run at high batch sizes (64–192 sequences) where draft-model verification wastes Tensor Core cycles; reserve speculative decoding strictly for low-batch latency tiers.

  5. Isolate RDMA Control Sockets Behind Cluster NetworkPolicies: Never expose NIXL/UCX sideband coordination ports outside the dedicated GPU pod subnet, and model your hardware savings in our Sovereign MoE Silicon X-Ray & Cloud GPU Repatriation Calculator before ordering additional racks.

When Should You Use Disaggregated Prefill-Decode Instead of Chunked Prefill?

Chunked prefill works well on single-node deployments (1–8 GPUs) with moderate input lengths (< 8,192 tokens) and relaxed Inter-Token Latency budgets (p99 ITL > 80 ms). You should switch to disaggregated prefill-decode via NixlConnector once you operate multi-node clusters serving long-context workloads (16K–128K tokens) under strict streaming SLAs (p99 ITL < 40 ms), where colocated prefill interference wastes over 40% of cluster goodput.

Does Disaggregated Serving Require InfiniBand, or Does RoCEv2 Work?

Both InfiniBand and RoCEv2 (RDMA over Converged Ethernet) are supported natively by NVIDIA NIXL via its UCX transport backend. On 200 Gbps or 400 Gbps RoCEv2 fabrics configured with Priority Flow Control (PFC) and Explicit Congestion Notification (ECN), GPUDirect RDMA transfers a 2 GB FP8 KV cache between nodes in under 42 milliseconds with zero packet loss.

How Do LMCache and NixlConnector Work Together in vLLM V1?

NixlConnector provides the low-level asynchronous HBM-to-HBM and storage-to-HBM data-movement engine, while LMCache acts as as the distributed KV cache manager across shared system prompts and multi-turn agent histories. Pairing LMCache with NIXL lets Prefill nodes pull warm RAG document KV blocks from NVMe or pooled host DRAM at wire speed instead of recomputing attention from scratch.
