Video latency affects manual operation. For UI automation, do not rely on fixed sleep timers. Write assertions based on page state, since waiting time is determined by page loading speed, device load and control connection quality.

This lab uses Redroid for the Android runtime and scrcpy to view and control the screen. A browser console, tenant permissions, WebRTC gateway and billing system require extra implementation.

3 Deploying Your First Redroid Instance on a Linux Server

Check the Host Requirements First

Redroid runs on the Linux host kernel. Prepare a Linux host where you can manage kernel modules and run privileged containers, and install Docker Engine. For learning, you can start with 4 CPU cores, 8 GB of RAM, and an SSD. Determine actual capacity through load tests.

Redroid's kernel requirements include Binder, binderfs, ashmem or memfd, and corresponding memory allocation capabilities. The official docs also require a 4 KB page size. Verify these ahead of time, especially on ARM cloud servers. Docker Desktop’s underlying Linux VM must satisfy the same requirements.

Run these checks on your server:

uname -m
uname -r
getconf PAGE_SIZE
docker version

# Load the Binder driver
sudo modprobe binder_linux devices="binder,hwbinder,vndbinder"

# Check binderfs support
grep -w binder /proc/filesystems

If you get Module binder_linux not found, install the matching kernel modules extra package on Ubuntu:

sudo apt-get update
sudo apt-get install -y "linux-modules-extra-$(uname -r)"
sudo modprobe binder_linux devices="binder,hwbinder,vndbinder"

Package names differ for cloud-customized kernels. Follow Redroid official deployment docs for your distribution. Kernel version alone is not enough to guarantee Android image compatibility.

Create the Container and Persist Its Data

Create a lab directory, save this as start-phone.sh

#!/usr/bin/env bash
set -euo pipefail

PHONE_NAME="cloudphone-01"
PHONE_PORT="15555"
PHONE_IMAGE="redroid/redroid:12.0.0-latest"
PHONE_DATA_DIR="${PWD}/data/${PHONE_NAME}"

mkdir -p "$PHONE_DATA_DIR"
docker pull "$PHONE_IMAGE"

docker run -d \
  --name "$PHONE_NAME" \
  --restart unless-stopped \
  --privileged \
  --cpus="2" \
  --memory="3g" \
  -p "127.0.0.1:${PHONE_PORT}:5555" \
  -v "${PHONE_DATA_DIR}:/data" \
  "$PHONE_IMAGE" \
  androidboot.use_memfd=true \
  androidboot.redroid_width=720 \
  androidboot.redroid_height=1280 \
  androidboot.redroid_dpi=320 \
  androidboot.redroid_gpu_mode=guest

docker ps --filter "name=${PHONE_NAME}"

Run it with

bash start-phone.sh

Key parameters explained:

  • /data volume: Persist app data separately for each instance
  • 127.0.0.1:15555:5555: ADB only binds to loopback; use SSH forwarding for remote access
  • guest: Software rendering, good for initial verification
  • --cpus / --memory: Resource limits, tune based on your workload

After first deployment, use these commands to start/restart:

docker start cloudphone-01
docker restart cloudphone-01

Once validated, pin the image digest to avoid unexpected updates:

docker image inspect redroid/redroid:12.0.0-latest \
  --format '{{json .RepoDigests}}'

Connect Through ADB and Confirm Android Has Finished Booting

Install platform tools:

sudo apt-get update
sudo apt-get install -y adb python3 python3-venv

python3 --version
adb version
adb start-server
adb connect 127.0.0.1:15555
adb devices -l

adb -s 127.0.0.1:15555 shell getprop sys.boot_completed
adb -s 127.0.0.1:15555 shell getprop ro.build.version.release
adb -s 127.0.0.1:15555 shell getprop ro.product.cpu.abilist

Important: adb devices only confirms ADB transport. Wait for sys.boot_completed=1 before running automation.

Access the Server Instance from Your Local Computer

Start SSH port forwarding (keep this terminal open):

ssh -NT \
  -o ExitOnForwardFailure=yes \
  -o ServerAliveInterval=30 \
  -L 127.0.0.1:15555:127.0.0.1:15555 \
  your_user@your_server

Then connect locally and view screen with scrcpy:

adb connect 127.0.0.1:15555
scrcpy -s 127.0.0.1:15555 --max-size=1024 --max-fps=15

4 Organizing ADB Commands into a Reusable Python Module

Save as adbkit.py

from pathlib import Path
import shlex
import subprocess
import time

def run_adb(*args: str, serial: str | None = None,
            timeout: float = 15) -> bytes:
    command = ["adb"]
    if serial is not None:
        command.extend(["-s", serial])
    command.extend(args)

    try:
        result = subprocess.run(
            command,
            capture_output=True,
            timeout=timeout,
            check=False,
        )
    except subprocess.TimeoutExpired as exc:
        raise TimeoutError(f"ADB command exceeded {timeout:.1f} seconds") from exc

    if result.returncode != 0:
        message = (result.stderr or result.stdout).decode(
            "utf-8", errors="replace"
        ).strip()
        raise RuntimeError(message[:2000] or "ADB command failed")
    return result.stdout

class Device:
    def __init__(self, serial: str):
        self.serial = serial

    def shell(self, *args: str, timeout: float = 15) -> str:
        output = run_adb(
            "shell", shlex.join(args),
            serial=self.serial, timeout=timeout,
        )
        return output.decode("utf-8", errors="replace").strip()

    def wait_ready(self, timeout: float = 120) -> None:
        deadline = time.monotonic() + timeout
        last_error = "Android is booting"

        def remaining() -> float:
            seconds = deadline - time.monotonic()
            if seconds <= 0:
                raise TimeoutError("Device wait time exhausted")
            return min(10, seconds)

        while time.monotonic() < deadline:
            try:
                run_adb("connect", self.serial, timeout=remaining())
                state = run_adb(
                    "get-state", serial=self.serial,
                    timeout=remaining(),
                ).decode().strip()
                booted = self.shell(
                    "getprop", "sys.boot_completed",
                    timeout=remaining(),
                )
                if state == "device" and booted == "1":
                    return
                last_error = f"state={state}, boot_completed={booted!r}"
            except (RuntimeError, TimeoutError) as exc:
                last_error = str(exc)

            time.sleep(max(0, min(2, deadline - time.monotonic())))

        raise TimeoutError(f"Boot wait timed out for {self.serial}, {last_error}")

    def screenshot(self, destination: Path) -> None:
        png = run_adb(
            "exec-out", "screencap", "-p",
            serial=self.serial, timeout=20,
        )
        if not png.startswith(b"\x89PNG\r\n\x1a\n"):
            raise RuntimeError("Device returned an invalid PNG screenshot")
        destination.write_bytes(png)

This module handles connection retries, boot waiting, timeouts, and binary-safe screenshot capture.

5 Validating a Single Device Before Scaling to Multiple Devices

Save as fleet.py

import argparse
from concurrent.futures import ThreadPoolExecutor, as_completed
from datetime import datetime
import json
from pathlib import Path
import re
import time
from uuid import uuid4

from adbkit import Device, run_adb

def inspect_one(serial: str, output_dir: Path) -> dict:
    started = time.monotonic()
    output_dir.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)
    device = Device(serial)
    result = {
        "serial": serial,
        "ok": False,
        "artifacts": str(output_dir),
    }

    try:
        device.wait_ready(timeout=120)
        package_path = device.shell("pm", "path", "com.android.settings")
        if not package_path.startswith("package:"):
            raise RuntimeError("Image is missing com.android.settings")

        launch_output = device.shell(
            "am", "start", "-W", "-a", "android.settings.SETTINGS",
            timeout=30,
        )
        if "Error:" in launch_output:
            raise RuntimeError(launch_output)
        device.shell("pidof", "com.android.settings")
        device.screenshot(output_dir / "screen.png")
        result["ok"] = True
    except Exception as exc:
        result["error"] = f"{type(exc).__name__}: {exc}"
        capture_errors = []
        try:
            device.screenshot(output_dir / "failure.png")
        except Exception as capture_exc:
            capture_errors.append(f"Screenshot collection failed, {capture_exc}")
        try:
            logs = device.shell(
                "logcat", "-d", "-t", "200", timeout=15,
            )
            (output_dir / "logcat.txt").write_text(logs, encoding="utf-8")
        except Exception as capture_exc:
            capture_errors.append(f"Log collection failed, {capture_exc}")
        result["capture_errors"] = capture_errors

    result["elapsed_seconds"] = round(time.monotonic() - started, 2)
    return result

def main() -> int:
    parser = argparse.ArgumentParser(description="Concurrent Android device health checks")
    parser.add_argument("--serials", nargs="+", required=True)
    parser.add_argument("--workers", type=int, default=2)
    args = parser.parse_args()
    if args.workers < 1:
        parser.error("--workers must be greater than 0")

    serials = list(dict.fromkeys(args.serials))
    run_adb("start-server", timeout=20)
    run_name = datetime.now().strftime("%Y%m%d_%H%M%S")
    run_dir = Path("artifacts") / f"{run_name}_{uuid4().hex[:8]}"
    run_dir.mkdir(parents=True)
    results = []

    with ThreadPoolExecutor(max_workers=min(args.workers, len(serials))) as pool:
        futures = {}
        for index, serial in enumerate(serials, start=1):
            safe_name = re.sub(r"[^a-zA-Z0-9_.-]", "_", serial)[:80]
            device_dir = run_dir / f"{index:03d}_{safe_name}"
            future = pool.submit(inspect_one, serial, device_dir)
            futures[future] = serial

        for future in as_completed(futures):
            serial = futures[future]
            try:
                result = future.result()
            except Exception as exc:
                result = {
                    "serial": serial,
                    "ok": False,
                    "error": f"{type(exc).__name__}: {exc}",
                }
            results.append(result)
            with (run_dir / "results.jsonl").open("a", encoding="utf-8") as file:
                file.write(json.dumps(result, ensure_ascii=False) + "\n")
            print(json.dumps(result, ensure_ascii=False), flush=True)

    results.sort(key=lambda item: item["serial"])
    (run_dir / "summary.json").write_text(
        json.dumps(results, ensure_ascii=False, indent=2), encoding="utf-8",
    )
    succeeded = sum(item["ok"] for item in results)
    print(f"Checks complete, {succeeded}/{len(results)} succeeded, artifacts in {run_dir}")
    return 0 if succeeded == len(results) else 1

if __name__ == "__main__":
    raise SystemExit(main())

Test single device:

python3 fleet.py --serials 127.0.0.1:15555 --workers 1

Add Two Instances and Run Checks Concurrently

#!/usr/bin/env bash
set -euo pipefail

for index in 2 3; do
  name="$(printf 'cloudphone-%02d' "$index")"
  port="$((15554 + index))"
  data_dir="${PWD}/data/${name}"
  mkdir -p "$data_dir"

  docker run -d \
    --name "$name" \
    --restart unless-stopped \
    --privileged \
    --cpus="2" \
    --memory="3g" \
    -p "127.0.0.1:${port}:5555" \
    -v "${data_dir}:/data" \
    redroid/redroid:12.0.0-latest \
    androidboot.use_memfd=true \
    androidboot.redroid_width=720 \
    androidboot.redroid_height=1280 \
    androidboot.redroid_dpi=320 \
    androidboot.redroid_gpu_mode=guest
done

Forward multiple ports locally:

ssh -NT \
  -o ExitOnForwardFailure=yes \
  -o ServerAliveInterval=30 \
  -L 127.0.0.1:15555:127.0.0.1:15555 \
  -L 127.0.0.1:15556:127.0.0.1:15556 \
  -L 127.0.0.1:15557:127.0.0.1:15557 \
  your_user@your_server

Run concurrent health check:

python3 fleet.py \
  --serials 127.0.0.1:15555 127.0.0.1:15556 127.0.0.1:15557 \
  --workers 2

Important: At scale, add device lease / distributed lock to avoid race conditions.

6 Writing UI-Level Business Workflows with uiautomator2

Install dependencies:

python3 -m venv .venv
source .venv/bin/activate
python -m pip install --upgrade pip
python -m pip install 'uiautomator2>=3,<4' requests
python -m uiautomator2 version

Dump UI hierarchy:

from pathlib import Path
import uiautomator2 as u2

device = u2.connect("127.0.0.1:15555")
Path("hierarchy.xml").write_text(device.dump_hierarchy(), encoding="utf-8")
device.screenshot("current-screen.png")
print("Saved hierarchy.xml and current-screen.png")

Save login workflow as login.py

import argparse
from getpass import getpass
from pathlib import Path
from uuid import uuid4

import uiautomator2 as u2

from adbkit import Device

def login(serial: str, package: str, account: str, password: str) -> None:
    Device(serial).wait_ready(timeout=120)
    device = u2.connect(serial)
    device.implicitly_wait(10)
    artifact_dir = Path("artifacts") / f"login_{uuid4().hex}"
    artifact_dir.mkdir(parents=True)

    try:
        device.app_start(package, stop=True)
        username_field = device(resourceId=f"{package}:id/username")
        password_field = device(resourceId=f"{package}:id/password")
        login_button = device(resourceId=f"{package}:id/login")

        if not username_field.wait(timeout=20):
            raise TimeoutError("Login page loading timed out")

        username_field.set_text(account)
        password_field.set_text(password)
        login_button.click()

        home = device(resourceId=f"{package}:id/home_title")
        if not home.wait(timeout=20):
            raise TimeoutError("Expected home-page control did not appear after login submission")

        print(f"[{serial}] Post-login page assertion passed")
    except Exception:
        try:
            device.screenshot(str(artifact_dir / "failure.png"))
        except Exception as exc:
            print(f"Failed to capture failure screenshot, {exc}")
        try:
            (artifact_dir / "hierarchy.xml").write_text(
                device.dump_hierarchy(), encoding="utf-8",
            )
        except Exception as exc:
            print(f"Failed to collect UI hierarchy, {exc}")
        raise

def main() -> None:
    parser = argparse.ArgumentParser()
    parser.add_argument("--serial", required=True)
    parser.add_argument("--package", required=True)
    args = parser.parse_args()
    account = input("Test account ").strip()
    password = getpass("Test password ")
    login(args.serial, package, account, password)

if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

Run:

python login.py --serial 127.0.0.1:15555 --package com.example.demo

7 Keeping a Clear Device Model When Integrating a Provider's OpenAPI

Save as cloud_api.py

from dataclasses import dataclass
import os

import requests

@dataclass(frozen=True)
class CloudPhone:
    instance_id: str
    serial: str

class ExampleCloudClient:
    def __init__(self, base_url: str, session: requests.Session):
        if not base_url.startswith("https://"):
            raise ValueError("OpenAPI URL must use HTTPS")
        self.base_url = base_url.rstrip("/")
        self.session = session

    def list_running(self, max_pages: int = 100) -> list[CloudPhone]:
        phones = {}
        for page in range(1, max_pages + 1):
            response = self.session.get(
                f"{self.base_url}/v1/instances",
                params={"page": page, "page_size": 50},
                timeout=(5, 20),
            )
            response.raise_for_status()
            payload = response.json()
            items = payload["items"]
            has_more = payload["has_more"]
            if not isinstance(items, list) or not isinstance(has_more, bool):
                raise ValueError("Invalid instance list response format")

            for item in items:
                if item["status"] == "RUNNING" and item.get("adb_endpoint"):
                    phone = CloudPhone(
                        instance_id=item["id"], serial=item["adb_endpoint"],
                    )
                    phones[phone.instance_id] = phone

            if not has_more:
                return list(phones.values())

        raise RuntimeError("Pagination limit exceeded, check the API pagination contract")

if __name__ == "__main__":
    with requests.Session() as session:
        session.headers["Authorization"] = f"Bearer {os.environ['CLOUD_API_KEY']}"
        client = ExampleCloudClient(os.environ["CLOUD_API_URL"], session)
        phones = client.list_running()
        print(f"Retrieved {len(phones)} running instances")

Best practice: Isolate provider API logic into this layer, keep your core automation code unchanged.

8 Troubleshooting Along the Pipeline

Symptom Check first Diagnostic steps
Container exits after starting Kernel capabilities, image arch, memory limits docker logs cloudphone-01
ADB connection refused Container status, port mapping, SSH forward docker port cloudphone-01 5555/tcp
ADB online but app won’t launch Boot status, package name getprop sys.boot_completed + pm path
APK install ABI error APK native libs vs image ABI getprop ro.product.cpu.abilist
UI element never found Current page, dialogs, custom view Save screenshot + dump_hierarchy()
Timeouts spike under concurrency Host load, memory, I/O docker stats --no-stream

Common debug commands:

docker logs --tail 100 cloudphone-01
docker inspect cloudphone-01 --format '{{json .State}}'
docker port cloudphone-01 5555/tcp
docker stats --no-stream

adb -s 127.0.0.1:15555 shell getprop sys.boot_completed
adb -s 127.0.0.1:15555 shell pm path com.android.settings
adb -s 127.0.0.1:15555 shell logcat -d -t 200

9 Choosing Between Self-Hosting and Managed Services

Self-host Redroid gives you full control over images and access, but you take responsibility for kernel compatibility, capacity planning and failure recovery. Managed cloud phones offload infrastructure work, and you evaluate reliability, API, cost and data isolation.

Evaluate with these dimensions:

  • App compatibility: Android version, ABI, GPU, required system services
  • Automation access: ADB auth, credential TTL, rate limits, async task API
  • Batch management: Bulk APK install, instance grouping, permission
  • Continuous operation: Success rate, recovery time under load
  • Data & cost: Isolation, backup, storage / traffic billing

Final Thoughts

After finishing this lab, you get persistent Android instances, ADB access, and batch health check scripts that capture screenshots and logs on failure.

When scaling, define business assertions first, then add task queues, device leases and failure recovery. Reliable large-scale automation is not about clicking, it is about verifying device state and preserving failure evidence.

title: AI-Generated Playwright Tools: 1 in 4 Runs Returned Wrong Data With No Error
description:
Tools that turn a website into an API for an AI agent often generate Playwright code and repair it when it fails. On a recent Launch HN thread, commenters asked two questions about this: can a tool return success when the action never completed, and does anything notice when a field goes empty while the response still looks fine?

I measured it. I changed an orders page in 10 ways and ran 3 AI-generated tools against the baseline and each changed version, with a repair loop. In 16 of 66 runs (16 of the 60 on a changed page) the tool returned wrong data and reported success. The repair loop never saw those runs, because it only starts on an error. A schema check plus four checks against the page turned all 16 into errors, and the repair loop could then work on them.

The code, every generated tool and every run are in the PoC repo.

The setup

The site is a small orders page: 12 orders, 8 of them open, with a Cancel button on each row. The page loads its data from an API. There is a baseline version and 10 changed versions:

Change What the page or API does
css-rename every class and container id renamed
column-swap Customer and Total columns swapped
locale-format totals shown as 1.234,50 € in place of €1,234.50
api-rename the API field total renamed to amount; the page shows —
late-rows the API answers after 2.5 s; placeholder rows until then
paginated 5 orders per page, with a Next page button
soft-error HTTP 200, an error banner, no rows
cancel-409 the cancel API refuses with 409, but the page still says "Order cancelled"
cancel-confirm Cancel opens a confirm dialog
card-layout cards in place of the table

Each tool has two tasks: list the open orders (id, customer, total), and cancel order A-1003.

  • Generation: claude -p --model sonnet writes the tool from the rendered HTML of the baseline page. I did this 3 times, so there are 3 different tools. The model gets the task prompt and the HTML: no tools, no project files, no CLAUDE.md.
  • Repair: when a run fails with an error, the model gets the error, the code and the HTML of the changed page, and writes a new version. Up to 2 repairs per run.
  • Scoring: each run is checked against the server's data. Correct, loud (an error), or silent (no error, wrong result). For the error banner and the refused cancel, an error is the correct result.

The results

Arm Runs Correct Loud Silent
Generated, with repair 66 45 5 16
+ schema check 66 46 7 13
+ checks against the page 66 58 8 0

66 runs per arm: 3 tools, the baseline plus 10 changes, 2 tasks. The repair loop worked when it got an error: in the first arm, all 16 repaired runs ended correct or with an error, never silent. What it never got was the 16 silent runs.

What the silent runs returned

Change Silent (of 3) What the tool returned
locale-format 3 1.234,50 € read as 1.2345, 420,00 € as 42000
cancel-409 3 cancelled: true, but the order is still open
api-rename 3 every total 0
late-rows 2 an empty list
soft-error 2 an empty list
card-layout 2 an empty list
css-rename 1 an empty list

Most come from a line that turns a failure into a value. These two are from the third generated tool:

return Number.isNaN(n) ? 0 : n;                                       // a missing total becomes 0
await page.waitForSelector(ROW, { timeout: 10000 }).catch(() => {});  // a timeout becomes an empty list

The other two tools got the totals of 0 another way: they strip — to an empty string, and Number("") is 0.

All 3 money parsers removed the commas before they parsed the number, so the German format lost its decimal point. All 3 cancels counted as done when the row left the page. On cancel-409 the page removes the row even though the server refused, so each tool saw what it expected.

The common thread is code that prefers a value to an error, and a repair loop that waits for an error never sees it.

What caught them

A schema check on the output (id and customer not empty, total a positive number) caught the 3 runs with totals of 0, and nothing else. An empty list is a valid list. 1.2345 is a positive number.

Four checks against the page, run after the schema, caught the other 13:

  1. The page shows no error banner (role="alert").
  2. The page's "N open orders" count equals the number of orders the tool returned.
  3. The digits of each total match the digits in that row on the page.
  4. After a cancel, a reload shows one open order less, and no row for that id.

With the schema and these checks, no run was silent. Of the 16 runs that had been silent:

  • 8 were repaired to the correct result (locale-format 3, late-rows 2, card-layout 2, css-rename 1).
  • 5 ended with an error, which is the correct result for the error banner and the refused cancel.
  • 3 (api-rename) still failed after 2 repairs, with an error.

Across the arm, 27 runs needed a repair: 19 ended correct and 8 ended with an error (api-rename 3, cancel on the error page 3, cancel with late rows 2).

One check was wrong. On api-rename, two repaired tools read the correct totals from the API, but the page shows —, so check 3 failed them. I count those as errors, not as silent failures.

The limits

  • I wrote the checks after I saw which runs failed silently in the first two arms. They check general things (an error on the page, a count, the digits, a re-read after an action), but they know this page's count label and row markup. Another site needs its own.
  • Three tools from one model, two tasks, one small page. The rates are for this setup, not for any product.
  • The changes are mine, and all of them at once is not how a real site changes.
  • The generated code is saved, so a re-run gives the same numbers. A new generation can give different code.

The repo also has a hand-written tool with Playwright assertions. It had no silent failures in 22 runs, but I wrote it knowing the changes, so it is not a fair comparison.

What I'd do with it

  • If a tool repairs itself on errors, check that it fails when it should. Count the silent results, not the repairs.
  • Search the generated code for lines that turn an error into a value. In these tools: .catch(() => {}) on a wait, isNaN(n) ? 0 : n, and Number() on text that can be empty.
  • Add at least one check that comes from the page and not from the tool: a count the page shows, or a re-read after an action.
  • Treat a schema check as the floor. It catches missing values, not wrong ones.

Repo: qa-gary-parker/poc-ai-tool-silent-failures. The self-healing tests experiment and the mutation testing experiment look at the same problem from the test side. More are in the playbook.

Originally published at https://garyparker.dev/blog/ai-generated-playwright-tools-silent-failures
